label: text
text: KOWLOON TONG EVENTS.

label: paragraph_title
text: Charge.

label: text
text: Alleging that on the instigation of Mr. A. E. Murphy, of the Kowloon Tong Development Company, they had been wrongfully arrested, falsely charged and detained for two or three hours, six collies engaged on the work of levelling ground at Kowloon Tong claimed $1,000 joint damages at the Summary Court this morning.

label: text
text: Alleged Wrongful Detention and

label: text
text: Mr. D. McCallum appeared for the "plaintiffs and Mr. R. A. Wadeson for Mr. Murphy, the defendant.

label: text
text: The plaintiffs' case was that one of the six coolies was proceeding from work at 5 p.m. on July 27, carrying some cement bags, the property of his employers, the Tung Lee Company. He was stopped by an Indian watchman employed by the Kowloon Tong Development Company and accused of stealing the bags.

label: text
text: The coome was then taken to the house of Mr. Murphy at 47 Kowloon Tong and Mr. Murphy ordered his detention. The Tung Lee Company, said Mr. McCallum, had a contract with the Government for levelling certain ground at Kowloon Tong. Mr. Murphy was employed by the Kowloon Tong Development Co. which had nothing whatsoever to do with the Tung Lee.

label: paragraph_title
text: Workmen Protest.

label: text
text:
Certain of the fellow workmen of "the man who was detained by Mr. Murphy went to the house to enquire into the cause of his detention and to protest. They also, it was alleged, had been detained and abused "within degree."
Later, the police went to the scene, continued Mr. McCallum, presumably on information lodged by Mr. Murphy; the men were handcuffed, somewhat roughly handled, a revolver pointed at them and marched through the streets. "It was not until eight o'clock that they were released on the order of the police. " Subsequently, a letter was written to Mr. Murphy on behalf of the plaintiffs (by Messrs. Leo d'Almada and Mason) in which it was stated that the men were acting only in the course of their employment, that Mr. Murphy had obtained a revolver from his wife and, pointing at one of the men, had roughly pushed him towards his (Mr. Murphy's) office, at the same time directing the Indian watchmen to take the others to the same place. This, stated the letter, the watchmen had done, covering the workmen with their rifles in the meantime. After investigation of the charge the police had ordered their release. The letter concluded that it was difficult to understand such conduct and intimated that unless redress was made proceedings would be instituted.

label: text
text: To this letter there had been no reply, stated Mr. McCallum.

label: paragraph_title
text: Police Evidence.

label: text
text:
Inspector Stimson, in charge of Kowloon City Police station, said that it was shortly after 6 p.m. on the day in question that he got to the charge room. The six plaintiffs were there in the dock in charge of Indian watchmen. Mr. Murphy was not there and witness had difficulty in understanding what the charge against the men was. Some cement bags were produced which the plaintiffs were alleged to have stolen.
In reply to questions, Inspector Stimson said that the sergeant interpreter was in charge of the station during witness's absence and it would have been he who ordered them to be placed in the dock. So far as witness knew the men were not handcuffed when he saw them but it was the practice to take handcuffs off when placing people in the dock. Witness made an entry in the charge book.

label: text
text: Asked why he had done this if no charge had been formulated against the men, witness replied that he gathered from replies to questions put through interpreters that the men were charged with the theft of the bags.

label: text
text: Mr. Wadeson, in cross-examining, said that witness had made a

text: REAL GRIEVANCE?

label: text
text:
TENANTS GROUSE AGAINST
LANDLORD

label: text
text: $10 INCREASE

label: text
text: Part of the whole facts seem to have been concealed in a letter to the "China Mail," written by Yee Chan; formerly of No. 1. On Tai Street (ground floor).

label: text
text: Allegations of what amounts to "sharp practice" are made by Yee Chan against the owner's agent. If what the tenant says is true, he should have protected himself as provided by law, or he has his means of redress.

label: text
text: From what is known generally of similar chases, the “grouse” is most likely based on misunderstanding.

label: paragraph_title
text: Curious Factor

label: text
text: Yee Chan is a purveyor of roasted pork, "varnished" duck, etc.

label: text
text: His rent per month was $40 until the Rents Restriction Ordinance lapsed. Then the agent applied for an increase of $10 a month. This I acceded to but the agent did not come to collect the rent for two months.

label: text
text:
Several days ago, action was taken whereby my furniture and fittings were sold by auction and I was expelled from possession.
"After deducting accounts due, there was nothing paid to me from the proceeds, (of the auction?)"

label: paragraph_title
text: "I am Unlucky!"

label: text
text: It rent was owing, the agent was in his rights in sending the balliff round. The tenant maintains that no application was made to him for payment, the implication being that the arrears were not due to him. Did Yee Chan make any effort to pay the rent even if the agent did not go round to collect?

text: PEAK BURGLAR.

label: paragraph_title
text: PROPERTY STOLEN FROM EUROPEAN.

label: text
text: The residence of Mr. W. H. Bell, No. 374, the Peak, was broken into by a burglar on Saturday night.

label: text
text: Access was gained by breaking a pane of glass and opening a window of the dining room.

label: text
text: The thief took several articles of clothing valued at $10.50—belonging to Mr. Bell, and also part of the amah's valuables consisting of two pieces of jewellery and $32 in money.

label: text
text: At the Central Magistracy this morning, 'Sergeant' McEwen charged five men with gambling. It was stated that a card party was held on the roof of a house. They were fined $3 each.

label: text
text:

Cunningham who had mentioned to him something about trouble at Kowloon Tong in the course of which an attack had been made on some Indian watchmen.
Mr. Wadeson asked witness if it was not probable that he connected this with this appearance of the men in the charge room when he got there. Witness said that he might have thought of what he had been told. In reply to further questions he said he did not question the coolies or the watchmen as to the events of which he had heard.

label: text
text:
Mr. Wadeson put it to Inspector Stimson that it was in consequence of a telephone message from Mr. Rouse, of the P.W.D. and an interview with the manager of the Tung Lee that the men had been released and that it had been put to the police that it would be very impolitic not to release them as otherwise there might be a strike of all the men working on the Government nullah. Inspector Stimson said that the men had been released as there was no charge against them.
The plaintiffs' evidence and cross-examination occupied the whole of the morning and this afternoon the defence will open.

text: Since noon quietness has been reigning: — Reuter.

label: text
text: Swatow, there are now no pickets on these waterways.

label: text
text: The only boat the strikers had at Swatow has been taken over. It is assumed that the pickets have now fled.

label: text
text:
Hitherto passengers and cargo coolies going to and from British vessels at Canton and Swatow have had to run the gauntlet as the pickets opened fire indiscriminately. During the weekend, it has been made plain that such picketing will have to stop.
The “China Mail” also learns from an authentic source that monetary help for the strikers has been withheld during the last few days. The practice in the past, which has not been denied, was to give each striker 20 cents every ten days, and two meals a day; the pickets got a little more pay for their duties. It is understood that such help has not been forthcoming for two or three days.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: The vernacular paper state that the Cantonese recently sent an emissary to Sun Chuan-lang urging him to join the Southerners, but he refused all offers, declaring that he is strongly opposed to Bolshevism and Communism.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: STONES THROWN.

label: text
text: BRITISH LAND PARTY AT CANTON.

label: paragraph_title
text: WHARF INCIDENT

label: text
text: Armed British bluejacket and marines landed on the "two wharves of the Hongkong, Canton and Macno Steamboat Co., Ltd., at Canton, on Saturday, and ejected a party of strike pickets and others.

label: text
text: Stones were subsequently thrown, states a report which has reached the “China Mail,” but it is almost certain that the missiles were not directed at the landing party.

label: text
text: It is believed that in the pell-mell which ensued when the tres-passers rushed on to the western bund, a coolie carrying two-wine jar's was bowled over, and his aamshu lost through the containers breaking.

label: text
text: A "row" followed, a bully being jeered. Stones were thrown at the bully but not on to the wharf.

label: paragraph_title
text: Dining Room Upset?

label: text
text:
There are two wharves, similar in appearance, on the Bund, which are the property of the company. The space in between is also British owned. Ropes have now been secured between the two wharves to prevent people landing there.
A correspondent states that strike pickets have used the wharf as a refectory. This seems to be borne out by the observations of an eyewitness who saw the caterer to the strikers rapidly evacuating cooking utensils, bowls, chopsticks and "chow" that was in course of preparation for the evening meal.

label: text
text: It appears that the British Consul has been in negotiation with the Canton. Foreign Office about the occupation of the wharves—discussed since last year when the steamers anchored in the stream prevent agitators "getting at" the crews, etc.

label: paragraph_title
text: "Row" on the Bund.

label: text
text: The Strike Executive is reported to have issued orders for bidding their men to enter foreign buildings.

label: text
text: Till noon on Saturday, the trespassers were given to leave. About 2 m. p.m., several British gunboats steamed into position and parties were landed from armed launches. The sailors soon got to work and were in possession with little or no trouble.

label: text
text: Strike pickets were alleged to have fallen out with two pedestrians on the road. These men were taken by the police to a police station in the vicinity; from whence they are believed to have been forcibly removed to strike headquarters.

label: text
text: The “China Mail” learns that a man was subsequently found on the street with grievous wounds in his abdomen. It is said that the man was so badly cut that his organs fell out! He is surmised to have been mixed up in the “row” among the Chinese, on the bund, during the confusion.

label: text
text: This incident, lacks confirmation and is only given for what is worth.

label: paragraph_title
text: WAR THREATENS?

label: text
text: SWATOW OFFICIALS SAID TO BE LEAVING.

label: text
text: Lack of definite information precludes the possibility of an authentic statement on the "war" position at Swatow.

label: text
text: News from the spot is that the Cantonese officials are in a panic, having detained a China Merchants (Chinese flag) steamer in the harbour.

label: text
text: Other items point to the danger of an early attack:

label: text
text:
There is no confirmation of a local outbreak in the hinterland of Swatow, nor has any further news been received about the march of Fukien troops into Kwangtung.
Of Hongkong shipping companies, only the Osaka Shosen Kaisha is sending steamers there.

label: text
text: The comparatively small number of Canton troops in the district, due to the calls of the front, may have caused the panic but the march of Fukien troops southwards still lackl conformation. The Chinese Navy is still reported at Amoy and there are no signs of a sortie on Swatow. These warships have done very little in recent civil

label: paragraph_title
text: YANGTZE TRUTH:

label: paragraph_title
text: British Gunboats in Action.

label: paragraph_title
text: INCIDENTS EXPLAINED.

label: text
text: How B. and S. Steamer Came to

label: text
text: Details regarding the seizure of a Butterfield and Swire teamer on the Yangtse River, and the movements of certain British warships, have reached the "China Mail," throwing considerable light on the situation.

label: text
text: - Wan Hsien, where the steamer was seized, is far up the Yangtse River—beyond the war zone—in Szechuan province, which is ruled by General Yang Sen, nominally a subordinate of Wu Pei-fu.

label: text
text: The boat was surrounded by sampans at Wan Hsien, troops of Yang Sen trying to get on board the steamer. The ship was fired on and she then stopped in the river. The sampans containing the soldiers then collided and sank.

label: paragraph_title
text: Gunboats' Adventures.

label: text
text: General Yang alleges that the steamer ran "down the sampans and thereupon ordered the vessel to be seized.

label: text
text: H.M.S. "Cockchafer" proceeded to the scene but ran aground. She was subsequently fired on, presumably by troops from the banks.

label: text
text: Then H.M.S. "Widgeön" was sent along to do what was necessary.

label: text
text: H.M.'s Consul at Chungking has also gone along to Wan Hsien to settle the matter if possible. (Chungking is the last big "port" on the upper reaches of the Yangtse, also in Szechuan province)

label: text
text: As regards H.M.S. "Scarab," which was reported by Reuter to have been in action with southern troops for two hours, disconnected messages have reached Hong Kong. As far as can be made out, firing was opened at the gunboat from the shore and was replied to, as has been done on other occasions.

label: paragraph_title
text: MARITAL TROUBLE.

label: paragraph_title
text:
QUEER DEFENCE BY A HUSBAND.
THREAT TO KILL.

label: text
text: An extraordinary defence was put forward by a Chinese when he was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with causing grievous bodily injuries to his wife. He denied the assault, but stated that he had a Bamboo pole in his hand.

label: text
text: His Worship: And the bamboo pole happened to fall on her head? Defendant readily agreed to this suggestion.

label: text
text:
Divisional Inspector Blackman in a statement said that the woman was apparently the defendant's wife, and they had had a dispute between them. It was alleged by the woman that she was attacked with a hatchet, but he thought this was hardly consistent with her wounds.
Defendant was fined $5 and bound over to keep the peace.

label: text
text: On leaving court the woman informed the Magistrate that she had been threatened with death since his arrest. She was assured of protection by the police.
